title: Status Report
description: The weekly status report most junior PMs write badly. Two pages, scannable in ninety seconds, designed to surface what the reader needs to decide — not to prove the project is busy. Five sections, one of which is the only one a sponsor will read.

# [Programme name] — Status Report
_Week ending [date] · prepared by [name]_

## 1. Headline
_One sentence. RAG status + the one thing the reader needs to take away._

## 2. Decisions needed this week
_Bullets. If empty, say so explicitly — silence reads as 'I'm hiding something'._

## 3. Progress vs plan
| Workstream | Status | Was due | Next milestone |
|------------|--------|---------|----------------|
|            |        |         |                |

## 4. Risks + issues changed this week
_Only changes since last week. New, escalated, de-escalated, closed. Don't re-list the static register._

## 5. What's coming next week
_3 bullets max. The reader should be able to skim this and know what to ask about next Monday._

worked_examples.content_md:
# Customer Data Migration — Status Report
_Week ending 15 May 2026 · prepared by Adekunle Bello_

## 1. Headline

**AMBER.** Migration is on track for the 18 June go-live, but the QA window has shrunk to four days (was nine). Decision needed on whether to defer non-critical reports to Phase 2.

## 2. Decisions needed this week

- **Sponsor decision (Thursday, latest):** Defer the four non-critical reports from launch to Phase 2 (recommendation), or hold the date and reduce QA scope. The 4-day QA window cannot test all 17 reports to the standard we agreed.
- **Eng lead + Compliance:** Sign-off on the revised data-residency note. Sent Tuesday; no reply yet.

## 3. Progress vs plan

| Workstream | Status | Was due | Next milestone |
|------------|--------|---------|----------------|
| Data mapping | Done | 8 May | — |
| Migration scripts | Done | 12 May | — |
| Reconciliation tooling | In progress (80%) | 15 May | Complete 18 May (3-day slip) |
| QA | Not started | 18 May | Starts 21 May, 4-day window |
| Comms to end users | Drafted | 22 May | Send 1 June |

## 4. Risks + issues changed this week

- **New:** Reconciliation tooling delivery slipped 3 days (vendor-side issue). Impact: QA window shortens from 9 to 4 days. Drives the decision in §2 above.
- **Escalated:** Compliance data-residency note still open after one week. Risk to sign-off date if not closed by 22 May.
- **Closed:** Data-mapping risk closed; final review with engineering passed on 13 May.

## 5. What's coming next week

- Reconciliation tooling delivery (Friday).
- Compliance sign-off on data-residency note.
- QA kickoff, 21 May.

annotations.note: The headline is the only section a senior reader is guaranteed to see. RAG + one sentence + the decision they need to make. If the headline says AMBER and there's no decision-needed in §2, the reader knows you're hedging.

Decisions-needed-by-name-and-deadline is the highest-value section in the whole document. The cost of an undecided decision compounds; the cost of asking explicitly is zero. Always include this section. If genuinely no decision is needed, write 'None this week' rather than omitting — silence reads as ducking.

The 'Was due' column is the one PMs delete first when the project is behind. Don't. The table is honest about slippage by construction; trying to disguise it in prose just delays the conversation by one week.

Only *changes*. A static risk register that re-lists every risk every week trains stakeholders to skip the section. New / escalated / de-escalated / closed is the only useful framing for a weekly report.

common_mistakes: Headline as a list of activities ('completed scripting, started QA, drafted comms'). The headline is for decisions, not for proving you were busy. The activity log goes in §3.
Decisions-needed section omitted because 'nothing came up'. Either you're hiding something or you're not paying attention. Senior readers parse the absence; write 'None this week' explicitly if true.

Green-when-it-should-be-amber. Most rookie PMs over-state status because they're afraid of looking like they're failing. The opposite is true — amber early reads as competence; surprise-red two weeks later reads as a lack of control.
Re-listing the entire risk register every week. The reader needs *what changed*. The static register lives in the project workspace and is linked once at the top, not pasted in.
More than two pages. If the report can't be scanned in ninety seconds, you've written a project document, not a status report. Cut.

RAG without a definition. Every organisation defines green / amber / red slightly differently. If you've inherited the report, spend ten minutes finding the definition — and if there isn't one, write one in your first month.
variant_patterns: Monthly variant: add a §6 'Spend vs budget' table and a §7 'Headcount + capacity' note. Headline becomes month-over-month trend, not week-over-week.

Programme-of-programmes variant: §3 becomes a programme-level summary table with each constituent project rolled up. Detailed status reports per project live underneath as appendices, not in the body.

Board variant: §1 (headline) becomes a one-paragraph narrative rather than a bullet. §2 reframes 'decisions needed' as 'board decisions needed' — most weekly decisions get resolved before the board sees the report.
